parts.title: Part 1: University Accommodation and Tenancy Registration
parts.context: A conversation between an international postgraduate student and a university housing officer.
parts.audioTranscript:
[00:00] Officer: Good morning, Campus Living and Accommodation Services. My name is Gregory. How may I assist you today?
[00:06] Student: Good morning, Gregory. I'm calling to finalize my residential registration for the upcoming academic session. I received my conditional room allocation notice, but I need to confirm specific lease conditions and update my personal records.
[00:19] Officer: Certainly. Let me pull up your student file on the central registry. Could you state your full name and student identification reference?
[00:27] Student: Yes, my surname is Lin, spelled L-I-N, and my given name is Maya. My registration ID is ST-8492.
[00:36] Officer: Thank you, Maya. Yes, here it is: ST-8492. You have been provisionally assigned to Oakwood Court, located on the North Campus precinct.
[00:47] Student: That's wonderful. Could you confirm which specific room type has been designated? I requested a self-contained studio or an en-suite single.
[00:56] Officer: Your allocation is for an en-suite single room in Block C. You will have a private bathroom with a shower and toilet, while the kitchen and dining lounge are shared between four postgraduate residents.
[01:08] Student: That sounds ideal for my architectural design studies. What about utility charges and internet connectivity? Are they incorporated into the base monthly rate?
[01:18] Officer: Yes, unlimited fiber-optic broadband, water, and central heating are fully inclusive in the £620 monthly fee. However, please note that electricity usage exceeding £45 per quarter is billed separately.
[01:33] Student: Understood. And regarding laundry facilities on the premises?
[01:37] Officer: There is a 24-hour laundry pavilion on the ground level of Block B. Access is managed via an electronic smartcard. You will need to provide an initial refundable deposit of £15 to activate the card at reception.
[01:52] Student: That is very reasonable. When do official move-in arrivals commence for autumn postgraduates?
[01:58] Officer: The keys can be collected starting from September 18th. If you arrive prior to that date, you will need to arrange temporary guest housing.
[02:08] Student: September 18th matches my flight schedule perfectly. Is there a designated storage area for personal bicycles?
[02:15] Officer: Yes, there is a secure, CCTV-monitored bicycle shed located immediately adjacent to the West Gate. You must register the frame serial number with campus security to receive an electronic gate fob.
[02:29] Student: Excellent. Finally, what emergency contact number should I log on the tenancy agreement?
[02:35] Officer: Please provide the international landline or mobile of an immediate family member. Let me take down your guardian's contact details right now...
[02:44] Student: It is plus 44, 7700, 900382.
[02:51] Officer: +44 7700 900382 recorded. And what is your emergency contact's relation to you?
[02:58] Student: That is my uncle, Arthur Lin.
[03:02] Officer: Wonderful. I will dispatch the formal contractual pack to your university email address within twenty-four hours.
[03:09] Student: Thank you so much for your assistance, Gregory. Have a pleasant day.
[03:13] Officer: You too, Maya. Goodbye.

parts.title: Part 2: Orientation Briefing at the Silver Sands Marine Reserve
parts.context: A talk by the head conservation warden to a group of newly recruited community volunteers.
parts.audioTranscript:
[03:30] Warden: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen, and welcome to the Silver Sands Coastal and Marine Sanctuary volunteer induction. I am Dr. Alistair Vance, the senior environmental steward. Over the next six months, your contribution will be instrumental in preserving our fragile intertidal ecosystems. Before we distribute your field monitoring kits, allow me to outline our territorial zoning and seasonal biosecurity rules.
[03:56] The reserve encompasses four distinct sectors stretching across seven miles of littoral shoreline. The North Lagoon, designated as Sector Alpha, is our primary scientific sanctuary. From March 1st through to July 31st, public access and recreational kayaking are strictly prohibited because this zone supports the nesting colonies of the roseate tern, an endangered migratory seabird. Volunteers entering Sector Alpha must wear sanitized overshoes to prevent introducing fungal spores.
[04:32] Moving to the Central Dunes, this area features our newly renovated visitors' center and the solar-powered meteorological observatory. All volunteers will muster here at 08:30 every morning for the daily briefing. The dunes are highly vulnerable to coastal erosion. For this reason, foot traffic is confined exclusively to the elevated timber boardwalks. Walking directly upon the marram grass is a prosecutable offense, as the root networks alone prevent the sand banks from disintegrating during winter gales.
[05:07] The South Shingle Spit is where we carry out marine litter audits and cetacean surveys. Because of hazardous tidal surges around Dead Man’s Reef, nobody is permitted on the outer spit within two hours of high water. You will each be issued a laminated tide table and a VHF maritime radio tuned to Channel 16.
[05:31] Now, concerning equipment maintenance. When you return from sampling expeditions, your pH sensors and refractometers must be rinsed with distilled water, which is stored in the blue carboys in Workshop 3. Under no circumstances should municipal tap water be utilized, as its high mineral content calcifies the delicate optical lenses.
[05:54] In the event of discovering a stranded marine mammal, such as a harbor seal pup or harbor porpoise, the protocol is unequivocal: do not touch the animal or attempt to shepherd it back into the sea. Immediately erect a 30-meter perimeter cordon using the reflective stanchions, and phone the veterinary rapid response unit on emergency speed-dial 4. Crowding causes catastrophic cardiovascular distress in cetaceans.
[06:23] Let us now inspect the sector orientation chart on the projection display...

parts.title: Part 3: Academic Tutorial on Biomimetic Architecture
parts.context: Two postgraduates, Clara and Leo, discussing their seminar project with Professor Holbrook.
parts.audioTranscript:
[06:45] Professor: Good afternoon Clara, Leo. Let us review the revised draft of your research paper on structural biomimicry in contemporary urban architecture. Clara, let's begin with your analysis of the Eastgate Centre in Harare, Zimbabwe. What did your empirical data reveal regarding its thermal efficiency?
[07:05] Clara: Well Professor, what impressed us most was how faithfully Mick Pearce mirrored the internal convective venting of macrotermes bellicosus termite mounds. Traditional office blocks in tropical climates expend nearly 40 percent of their total power consumption on electromechanical air-conditioning. By employing concrete slab thermal mass that absorbs diurnal heat and purging it through rooftop chimneys via passive nocturnal draft, the Eastgate building reduced HVAC operating overheads by 35 percent relative to conventional glass towers.
[07:44] Leo: And what's particularly remarkable is that the capital expenditure saved on cooling machinery immediately offset the cost of constructing the specialized thermal chimneys. However, in our literature review, we noted that several architectural critics argued that the Harare archetype cannot be universally replicated in maritime climates with high relative humidity, where nocturnal radiative cooling is severely impeded.
[08:12] Professor: A very astute critique, Leo. Passive evaporative and convective cooling relies heavily on substantial diurnal temperature differentials—often 12 to 15 degrees Celsius—which oceanic regions simply do not experience. Now, what about your second case study: the Council House 2 building in Melbourne?
[08:33] Clara: In CH2, the design team borrowed principles from tree transpiration and bark micro-shading. They installed recycled timber louvers that automatically rotate with solar azimuth angles, combined with chilled-beam ceiling conduits. What fascinated us was the measurable impact on indoor air quality: VOC concentrations dropped by 60 percent, and municipal absenteeism among city council staff declined by 18 percent over the first triennium.
[09:05] Leo: Though we had a minor disagreement regarding the economic valuation of that productivity dividend. Clara felt the absenteeism metric should be highlighted as the primary justification for sustainable retrofits, whereas I contended that without rigorous carbon abatement data, corporate developers remain skeptical.
[09:27] Professor: Both dimensions have merit. Institutional investors prioritize kilowatt-hour savings, whereas corporate tenants focus on human capital retention. For your final submission, you should synthesize both metrics into a unified lifecycle cost-benefit matrix.
[09:44] Clara: Understood. Now regarding our final section on future prospects: self-healing concrete inspired by bacterial endospores. We are examining Bacillus pseudofirmus.
[09:56] Professor: That is cutting-edge. When micro-cracks form and moisture penetrates, the dormant bacteria metabolize calcium lactate nutrients, precipitating limestone calcite that seals the fissure within three weeks. Be sure to address the durability limitations when exposed to acidic industrial precipitation.
[10:18] Leo: We have already compiled laboratory durability curves from Delft University. We will incorporate that data by Friday.
[10:25] Professor: Excellent. I look forward to reading the finalized version.

parts.title: Part 4: Academic Lecture on Marine Bioluminescence and Photonic Adaptations
parts.context: A university lecture delivered by a marine biologist at the Institute of Oceanography.
parts.audioTranscript:
[10:45] Lecturer: In today's lecture, we examine one of the most evolutionarily widespread yet visually enigmatic biological phenomena on Earth: marine bioluminescence. In the aphotic bathypelagic zone, stretching from 1,000 to 4,000 meters below sea level where ambient sunlight is entirely extinguished, light production is not an eccentric biological anomaly; it is the dominant mode of ecological interaction, exhibited by an estimated seventy-five to eighty percent of pelagic organisms.
[11:18] At the molecular level, bioluminescent photon generation is an extraordinarily efficient chemiluminescent reaction that releases virtually no thermal energy. This 'cold light' is generated through the enzymatic oxidation of a light-emitting substrate universally termed luciferin, catalyzed by the specialized enzyme luciferase. In the presence of dissolved molecular oxygen, adenosine triphosphate (ATP), and frequently calcium cofactors, luciferin is oxidized into an excited oxyluciferin complex. As this molecule returns to its thermodynamic ground state, it discharges discrete quanta of visible light, typically in the blue-green spectral wavelength between 470 and 490 nanometers. This specific spectral band is evolutionarily favored because blue-green photons experience the absolute minimum absorption and scattering coefficients in saline seawater.
[12:15] Now, consider the diverse morphological functions of photophores—the specialized glandular organs containing these biochemical reagents. In predatory species such as the deep-sea anglerfish, Melanocetus johnsonii, bioluminescence serves as aggressive mimicry. A modified dorsal spine called the illicium terminates in a glowing esca containing billions of symbiotic Photobacterium. In the perpetual abyss, unsuspecting teleost prey are lured directly toward the luminescent beacon, straight into the predator's prehensile jaws.
[12:51] Conversely, for mesopelagic organisms inhabiting the twilight zone between 200 and 1,000 meters, bioluminescence is primarily an optical camouflage strategy termed counterillumination. Organisms such as the hatchetfish possess ventral banks of photophores directed downward. Photoreceptors on the dorsal side of the fish measure the intensity and spectral quality of downwelling celestial sunlight. The fish then adjusts its ventral emission to match this downwelling light perfectly. Consequently, an apex predator gazing upward from the ocean abyss sees no silhouette against the illuminated surface waters; the hatchetfish becomes optically transparent.
[13:38] Beyond predation and concealment, bioluminescence governs intra-species communication and reproductive synchronization. Certain species of ostracod crustaceans emit pulses of light in precise geometric constellations to attract conspecific mates. In coastal environments, dinoflagellate blooms exhibit shear-induced bioluminescence. When mechanical shearing forces—such as a crashing surf or the wake of a swimming predator—deform the dinoflagellate cell membrane, voltage-gated proton channels open, acidifying internal scintillons and triggering instantaneous flashes. This functions as a 'burglar alarm', illuminating the secondary predator and rendering it vulnerable to tertiary carnivores higher in the trophic pyramid.
[14:26] Finally, biotechnologists are harvesting green fluorescent protein (GFP) and luciferin genes for biomedical imaging. These molecular markers allow oncologists to track real-time cellular metastasis in mammalian tissue without invasive biopsy...

passages.title: The Hydraulic Ingenuity and Hydro-Ecological Collapse of Classic Maya Metropolises
passages.subheading: An investigation into how advanced aggregate sand filtration and paved catchment plazas sustained urban populations in the karst tropics before environmental vulnerability triggered abandonment.
passages.text:
Paragraph A
For generations, American and European mesoamericanists were baffled by an apparent ecological paradox: how did colossal Classic Maya urban centers such as Tikal, Calakmul, and Caracol sustain dense metropolitan populations exceeding sixty to eighty thousand inhabitants within the tropical karst interior of the Petén Basin? Unlike the great fluvial civilizations of antiquity—the Nile Valley, Mesopotamia along the Tigris and Euphrates, the Indus Basin, and the Yellow River plain—the central Maya lowlands possessed neither perennial surface streams nor accessible riverine valleys. Furthermore, the underlying Cretaceous limestone geological substrate was so intensely permeable that rainfall instantly drained into deep subterranean caverns, far beyond the reach of primitive hand-dug wells. Compounding these hydrological constraints was an unyielding climatic seasonality divided strictly into a six-month tropical deluge and a debilitating half-year drought during which water scarcity threatened daily human survival.

Paragraph B
Groundbreaking advances in airborne LiDAR remote sensing and geochemical analysis of sedimentary lake cores have illuminated the monumental hydraulic infrastructure designed to overcome these geographic liabilities. Rather than viewing the deluge as an uncontrollable hazard, Maya urban planners transformed entire city centers into vast, contiguous rainwater-harvesting apparatuses. Monumental acropolises, elevated ceremonial causeways known as sacbeob, and vast public plazas were intentionally paved with impermeable calcitic plaster and graded with subtle, micro-engineered slopes ranging from 0.5 to 2.0 degrees. These calculated gradients channeled millions of liters of torrential monsoon runoff through a network of masonry conduits straight into colossal, subterranean plastered reservoirs termed aguadas, ensuring municipal storage capacities that could withstand up to eighteen months of total rainfall cessation.

Paragraph C
Nevertheless, impounding millions of gallons of stagnant water within a sweltering tropical rainforest generated a lethal biological peril. In the absence of water circulation, warm tropical reservoirs rapidly become breeding incubators for pathogenic cyanobacteria, parasitic protozoans, and mosquito vectors transmitting debilitating fevers. In a landmark 2020 excavation conducted by geoarchaeologists from the University of Cincinnati at Tikal's Corriental reservoir, researchers unearthed the earliest known macroscopic water filtration apparatus in the Western Hemisphere. Strategically installed directly behind the masonry intake sluices was a multi-tiered filtration bed composed of alternating strata of coarse crystalline quartz sand and imported zeolitic volcanic aluminosilicate minerals.

Paragraph D
The presence of zeolite in a lowland sedimentary basin is of profound technological significance. Zeolite is an exceptionally porous volcanic mineral endowed with natural molecular-sieve properties and a strong negative electrostatic charge, enabling it to absorb toxic heavy metals, microbial bacteria, and hazardous organic tannins from cloudy runoff. Crucially, the nearest known geological source of this mineral is situated in the volcanic cordillera of the Bajo de Azúcar, more than thirty kilometers to the northeast of Tikal. The logistical effort required to quarry, pulverize, and transport metric tons of heavy volcanic minerals across rugged jungle terrain in the absence of wheeled draught carts or pack animals demonstrates an institutionalized civic commitment to municipal sanitation. Radiocarbon dating confirms that the Corriental filtration beds were maintained and periodically replenished for over seven centuries.

Paragraph E
Tragically, this extreme degree of centralized hydraulic hyper-engineering also sowed the seeds of civilizational vulnerability. Speleothem stalagmite isotope records from regional caves reveal that during the ninth and tenth centuries CE, Mesoamerica was gripped by a succession of catastrophic multi-year megadroughts linked to intertropical convergence zone shifts. As precipitation plummeted by up to fifty-four percent, the great civic reservoirs were repeatedly drawn down to their stagnant dregs. Geochemical sampling of Tikal's innermost palace reservoirs revealed lethal concentrations of mercury, leached from the cinnabar (mercuric sulfide) pigment extensively utilized by the royal court to coat temple facades and funerary vaults. When prolonged drought concentrated this toxic heavy metal in the sediment, the municipal water supply transformed into a lethal poison. Unable to sustain the urban workforce and facing environmental catastrophe, the ruling dynasties collapsed, and the great forest metropolises were permanently abandoned.

passages.title: Neuroplasticity, Executive Function, and the Cognitive Reserve of Multilingualism
passages.subheading: How active management of multiple linguistic codes restructures the prefrontal cortex, enhances attentional inhibition, and mitigates neurodegenerative decline.
passages.text:
Paragraph A
Throughout the early decades of the twentieth century, an entrenched pedagogical consensus in Western educational psychology maintained that exposing young children to bilingual environments was intrinsically detrimental. Prominent developmental researchers asserted that compelling a developing brain to assimilate two divergent lexicons and grammatical codes generated severe cognitive interference, delayed vocabulary acquisition, and contributed to permanent intellectual deficits. It was not until the seminal 1962 Montreal investigation conducted by Elizabeth Peal and Wallace Lambert that this deficit paradigm was dismantled. Using methodologically rigorous controls for socioeconomic status and parental education, Peal and Lambert demonstrated that bilingual children exhibited marked superiority over monolingual peers in non-verbal divergent thinking, symbolic manipulation, and conceptual flexibility.

Paragraph B
In the subsequent decades, structural and functional neuroimaging technologies—most notably functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) and Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI)—have unveiled the neurological mechanisms underpinning these performance differentials. Cognitive neuroscientists now recognize that in the multilingual brain, all known languages remain perpetually active simultaneously. Even when an individual is conversing exclusively in their native tongue, lexical candidates in their secondary and tertiary languages are continuously activated in parallel. The brain does not possess a mechanical compartmentalization switch that shuts down one lexicon while another is in use. Consequently, speech production necessitates an unrelenting mental competition that must be resolved through selective suppression.

Paragraph C
To prevent intrusive cross-linguistic errors and unintended code-switching, the brain continuously enlists the executive control network—a distributed fronto-basal-parietal circuitry centered in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, and basal ganglia. This apparatus governs domain-general executive functions: conflict monitoring, selective attention, working memory updating, and inhibitory control. Because bilingual individuals must exercise this inhibitory neuro-musculature in every conversational exchange, their executive network undergoes continuous neuroplastic adaptation. DTI neuroimaging reveals increased fractional anisotropy—a marker of enhanced white-matter myelin integrity—in the corpus callosum and superior longitudinal fasciculus of lifelong bilinguals, signifying faster and more robust neural signal transmission between hemispheres.

Paragraph D
This continuous mental conditioning manifests across behavioral paradigms measuring attentional control. In experimental tasks such as the Stroop color-word test, the Simon spatial incompatibility task, and the Flanker paradigm, participants must attend to a target stimulus while actively ignoring distracting or conflicting peripheral cues. Across diverse age demographics, bilingual subjects consistently demonstrate a significant reaction-time advantage, commonly referred to as the 'bilingual executive advantage.' Crucially, this cognitive edge is most pronounced not in young adults at the peak of their physiological cognitive capacity, but at the extreme poles of the lifespan: in developing toddlers and aging senior citizens whose executive reserves are either forming or undergoing natural biological attrition.

Paragraph E
Perhaps the most consequential clinical implication of lifelong multilingualism lies in the etiology of age-related neurodegenerative pathology. In comprehensive epidemiological research led by Dr. Ellen Bialystok and verified by independent neurology cohorts worldwide, lifelong bilingual patients diagnosed with probable Alzheimer's disease consistently displayed initial clinical symptoms of memory loss, disorientation, and functional decline four to five years later than monolingual cohorts with matched chronological age and socio-educational profiles. Astonishingly, when post-mortem neuropathological examinations and high-resolution computed tomography scans compared the physical brain tissue of these cohorts, bilingual patients exhibited substantially greater cortical atrophy, synaptic depletion, and amyloid-beta plaque deposition than monolinguals exhibiting identical symptom severity.

Paragraph F
This striking discrepancy between physical brain damage and clinical cognitive performance is explained through the concept of 'cognitive reserve.' Multilingualism does not operate as an immunological shield against the physiological initiation of neuropathology; rather, decades of coordinating competing linguistic networks construct alternative, highly resilient neural circuits. When neurodegenerative plaques destroy primary neuro-pathways, the multilingual brain seamlessly bypasses the lesions by rerouting information through redundant subcortical and contralateral connections. The brain continues to function effectively until the accumulated structural destruction reaches a catastrophic threshold, effectively buying elderly individuals years of autonomous, high-quality living.

passages.title: Algorithmic Urbanism and the Autonomous Mobility Transition
passages.subheading: Assessing how on-demand self-driving transport fleets could dismantle municipal asphalt real estate, reorganize suburban zoning, and test regulatory safety governance.
passages.text:
Paragraph A
Throughout the twentieth century, no single technological consumer artifact exercised a more despotic influence over the architectural morphology of metropolitan spaces than the privately owned internal combustion passenger vehicle. In contemporary Western cities, private automobiles stand entirely stationary for an average of ninety-five percent of their operational lifespans. To accommodate these multi-ton depreciating metal boxes, municipalities across North America, Europe, and Australasia have surrendered between twenty-five and forty percent of their finite land footprints to parking infrastructure: vast asphalt lots, subterranean garages, and multi-lane curbside allocations. This spatial subsidization of private automotive storage has driven catastrophic urban sprawl, hyper-inflated urban residential real estate prices, and created impermeable heat islands that exacerbate stormwater flooding.

Paragraph B
Urban transport economists and algorithmic systems theorists argue that the convergence of three foundational technological revolutions—autonomous driving systems (ADS), electric powertrains, and algorithmic on-demand ridesharing platforms—is on the verge of obsoleting the century-old paradigm of individual vehicle ownership. If an autonomous, Level 4 or Level 5 electric pod can be summoned via smartphone application and arrive at an urban resident's doorstep within ninety to one hundred and twenty seconds, the financial and logistical rationale for paying insurance, registration fees, maintenance, and parking leases for an idle personal vehicle vanishes. Transport models developed at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology indicate that a shared fleet of autonomous vehicles representing merely fifteen to twenty percent of the current private car population could comfortably accommodate one hundred percent of daily passenger trips in a metropolitan city like Singapore or Vienna.

Paragraph C
The spatial dividends of this transition would be transformative. Automated on-demand vehicles do not require parking within dense downtown central business districts; between passenger dispatches, vehicles can either continuously circulate, queue in peripheral suburban charging depots, or dynamically redistribute to anticipation zones predicted by machine learning demand models. Consequently, vast swathes of municipal parking real estate—estimated at tens of thousands of square hectares in major cities—could be reclaimed. Urban architects envision converting surface parking lots into high-density affordable housing, micro-parks, urban farming pavilions, and bioswales designed to absorb monsoon precipitation. Furthermore, because autonomous driving algorithms optimize vehicle spacing and virtually eliminate human driver reaction latency, arterial roadways could safely operate with significantly narrower lanes, allowing wide swaths of asphalt to be permanently retrofitted into protected cycle tracks and pedestrian avenues.

Paragraph D
However, critical urban geographers and transport planners caution that the autonomous mobility revolution is fraught with dangerous socio-environmental counter-effects, primarily the threat of induced travel demand. If travel time ceases to be an unrewarding cognitive chore and transforms into productive leisure or work time inside a rolling office, commuter tolerance for long-distance transit will expand exponentially. Suburban commuters might happily accept ninety-minute commutes if they can sleep, stream media, or conduct business conferences inside an autonomous pod. Paradoxically, this could stimulate a catastrophic new wave of super-sprawl into fragile agricultural hinterlands. Furthermore, if autonomous rides are priced at dirt-cheap marginal operational costs, commuters will inevitably defect away from high-capacity municipal public transit, such as subways and light-rail trains. The nightmare scenario envisioned by transport analysts is a city choked by millions of empty 'zombie vehicles' circling urban blocks between appointments to avoid off-site parking tariffs.

Paragraph E
Beyond urban planning dilemmas lies the daunting challenge of algorithmic liability and algorithmic safety validation. Human drivers in industrialized nations possess an aggregate baseline safety record of approximately one fatal collision per one hundred million vehicle miles traveled (VMT). To statistically prove that an autonomous algorithm surpasses human safety performance by even twenty percent would require testing autonomous fleets across billions of physical road miles—a multi-decade timeline that physical road testing alone cannot achieve. Autonomous developers have consequently pivoted toward high-fidelity physics-based simulation engines, where generative artificial intelligence subjects autonomous software to billions of edge-case scenarios: sudden blizzard conditions, camera-blinding solar glare, and unpredictable pedestrian incursions across poorly lit intersections.

Paragraph F
Ultimately, the societal success of autonomous mobility will depend on municipal regulatory governance rather than silicon valley software sophistication. Without stringent congestion pricing, per-mile vehicle travel taxes, and explicit mandates obligating shared vehicle occupancy, autonomous fleets will exacerbate the very gridlock they were heralded to solve. Forward-thinking cities must enact spatial quotas that actively prioritize mass transit corridors and penalize empty vehicle repositioning. The autonomous vehicle is not an autonomous panacea; it is a disruptive technological catalyst whose outcome will be determined by whether municipal governments subjugate it to human-centric urban design or once again surrender their cities to the automobile.
